rationale: Across published cohorts of isolated CLN3-associated retinal degeneration (RP101), affected individuals consistently lack the hallmarks of classic juvenile neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis (JNCL/Batten disease)—namely pediatric-onset epileptic seizures, progressive motor regression, and childhood-to-adolescent neurodegenerative dementia. Ku et al. (2017) followed 10 patients over 3 to 29 years (up to age 70) and Smirnov et al. (2021) evaluated 15 patients across 11 families without manifestation of classic CLN3-related pediatric neurodegeneration. While editorial caution (e.g., Traboulsi 2021) and extended follow-up reviews note that subtle or protracted psychiatric or adult-onset neurologic symptoms can occasionally appear in protracted CLN3 spectrum disorders, childhood systemic neuroregression and early epileptic encephalopathy are definitively absent in RP101 and clearly distinguish classic JNCL from isolated RP101.

evidence.text: In a cohort of 15 patients from 11 unrelated families harboring biallelic CLN3 pathogenic variants presenting with isolated/nonsyndromic inherited retinal disease, patients manifested either mild middle-age onset or severe earlier-onset rod-cone degeneration without the classic severe neurological manifestations of JNCL.

source.title: Retinal Phenotype of Patients With Isolated Retinal Degeneration Due to CLN3 Pathogenic Variants in a French Retinitis Pigmentosa Cohort
source.quote: A total of 15 cases from 11 unrelated families harboring biallelic CLN3 variants were identified. All patients presented with nonsyndromic IRD... All but 1, p.(Arg405Trp), CLN3 point variants and their genotypic associations were clearly distinct between juvenile neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis and retina-restricted disease.

evidence.text: Detailed clinical evaluation of 10 patients harboring CLN3 mutations with isolated nonsyndromic retinal dystrophy followed for 3 to 29 years demonstrated no classic JNCL neurologic decline or pediatric seizures.

source.title: Detailed Clinical Phenotype and Molecular Genetic Findings in CLN3-Associated Isolated Retinal Degeneration
source.quote: A multi-institutional case series of 10 patients who presented with isolated nonsyndromic retinal disease and mutations in CLN3. Patient ages ranged from 16 to 70 years; duration of follow-up ranged from 3 to 29 years... Of the 10 patients, 4 had a progressive late-onset rod-cone dystrophy, with a mean (range) age at onset of 29.7 (20-40) years, and 6 had an earlier onset rod-cone dystrophy, with a mean (range) age at onset of 12.1 (7-17) years.

evidence.text: A 50-year-old patient with non-syndromic retinal dystrophy presenting at age 36 with compound heterozygous CLN3 mutations lacked juvenile-onset neurological deficit.

source.title: Clinical and molecular characterization of non-syndromic retinal dystrophy due to c.175G>A mutation in ceroid lipofuscinosis neuronal 3 (CLN3)
source.quote: Mutation of the CLN3 gene, associated with juvenile neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis, has recently been associated with late-onset, non-syndromic retinal dystrophy. Herein we describe the multimodal imaging, immunological and systemic features of an adult with compound heterozygous CLN3 mutations.

evidence.text: Editorial analysis emphasizes that while predominant ocular phenotypes occur in CLN3-associated disease, long-term monitoring for potential non-ocular systemic or late neurologic associations is warranted, cautioning against premature absolute classification as purely isolated.

source.title: Hereditary systemic diseases can have a predominant ocular phenotype, but they are still systemic diseases

new_directions.question_text: Do long-term prospective cohorts of RP101 patients eventually develop mild, late-adult neuropsychiatric or cardiac manifestations of CLN3 deficiency?
new_directions.rationale: Certain systemic lysosomal/ceroid lipofuscinosis genes present along a continuous hypomorphic spectrum; longitudinal adult assessments are required to confirm if RP101 remains strictly non-syndromic across complete natural lifespans.
